source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Core claim: similarity is like analogy. Both rest on structural alignment of relational representations. Analogy shares relations and few attributes; literal similarity shares both; mere appearance shares attributes only.
numbers: Similarity space with two axes: attribute overlap and relational overlap (Figure 1). No new data in this part.
quote: In a fundamental sense, similarity is like analogy, in that both involve an alignment of relational structure
limits: Position article; relies on the authors' own earlier studies. Assumes representations are already relational; says little about where they come from.
agent_relevance: Analogy and similarity differ in degree, not kind. Comparing two examples should be steered by shared relations, not shared surface words.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Three constraints on a good alignment: parallel connectivity, one-to-one correspondence, and systematicity (prefer connected systems of relations). The Structure-Mapping Engine (SME) works in three stages: local identical-predicate matches, coalescing into consistent kernels, then merging into one or a few maximal mappings. It scores deep systems over shallow ones and projects candidate inferences.
numbers: SME usually returns two or three best interpretations. A cross-mapped pair (earth/moon) gets the relational reading over the object reading because its structural score is higher.
quote: Candidate inferences are only guesses: Their factual correctness must be checked separately.
limits: Needs hand-built predicate representations; assumes relational predicates are partly identical.
agent_relevance: Explicit recipe that code could mimic: match, group, merge, score, project inferences. Candidate inferences are guesses and must be checked separately (fits G2, G3).

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Alignable differences are differences tied to the common structure (snake vs fish in the same role). Nonalignable differences have no counterpart (a clog with nothing to match). Alignable differences are more salient. Prediction: it is easier to list differences for similar pairs than for dissimilar pairs.
numbers: Summary of Gentner & Markman 1994: 40 word pairs, 5 minutes. Total differences listed: similar M=11.4, dissimilar M=5.9. Alignable: similar M=9.0, dissimilar M=3.9.
limits: Numbers here are the authors' summary of the 1994 data (checked against the 1994 paper).
agent_relevance: Hotel-motel yields many differences; magazine-kitten yields few. Differences are only informative when the two items share a structure first.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Alignable differences should count more against similarity than nonalignable ones. Triad: an arrow-at-target scene. The option with an added bird (nonalignable) was chosen as more similar than the option where the arrow targets the bird (alignable).
numbers: One illustrative forced-choice triad, no counts given in the review.
limits: The review itself flags a confound (the target moves) and points to a control in the 1996 paper.
agent_relevance: A change to a role-filler inside the shared structure is a bigger change than an added extra.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Structural alignment is offered as a reconciliation of similarity-based and theory-based categorisation: if similarity is alignment over relations (e.g. bats bear live young), bats group with mammals, not birds. Comparison also fosters insight by highlighting commonalities, relevant differences and new inferences.
numbers: No numbers; argued case.
limits: Argument, not a test.
agent_relevance: Supports using comparison to find the relation that carries a category, not surface look.

source: Gentner & Markman (1994) Structural alignment in comparison: No difference without similarity
finding: Experiment 1: people list one difference for as many word pairs as possible in 5 minutes. They manage more high-similarity than low-similarity pairs, and the gap lies in alignable differences.
numbers: N=32 undergraduates for listing (plus 40 raters). 40 pairs, 20 high and 20 low similarity. Pairs with a difference: high M=11.44, low M=5.88, F(1,30)=31.88, p<.001. Alignable: high 8.97 vs low 3.88, F(1,30)=31.37, p<.001. Nonalignable: high 2.47 vs low 2.00, F(1,30)=1.39, ns. Scorer agreement 97%.
quote: If similarity comparisons involve structural alignment, then subjects should list more differences (and particularly more alignable differences) for similar pairs
limits: Fixed word list, college students, paper and pencil. Free choice of pairs could mean people pick easy pairs (tested in Exp 2).
agent_relevance: Counterintuitive: more shared structure gives more findable differences. Compare near variants, not far ones, to find what changes (S2).

source: Gentner & Markman (1994) Structural alignment in comparison: No difference without similarity
finding: Experiment 2 rules out the 'people pick the easy pairs' reading. Each person got one similarity level, all pairs in a column, no choice. The high-similarity advantage held again and came from alignable differences.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates (24 per condition), one dropped for listing commonalities. Total differences high M=18.42 vs low M=13.79, t(46)=2.69, p<.01. Alignable high 15.63 vs low 11.54, t(46)=2.06, p<.05. Nonalignable high 2.79 vs low 2.25, t(46)=-0.47, ns. Scorer agreement 98%.
limits: Smaller effect between subjects: about 4.6 more differences against 5.6 in Exp 1. The authors leave open that other instructions could reverse it.
agent_relevance: The effect survives the self-selection worry but is modest and tied to word pairs.

source: Gentner & Markman (1994) Structural alignment in comparison: No difference without similarity
finding: Summary of earlier work (Markman & Gentner 1993a): more commonalities listed for similar pairs; total differences roughly constant across similarity; alignable differences up with similarity, nonalignable up with dissimilarity. Commonality counts correlated with alignable counts, not nonalignable counts. Slovic & MacPhillamy (1974) is cited: people weigh scores on the test both students took more.
numbers: Exact numbers are in the 1993 paper, which was not opened. No numbers for the Slovic result.
limits: Second-hand for the 1993 and Slovic studies.
agent_relevance: Alignable differences are dimensions on which both items already agree; decision weight is biased toward them.

source: Markman & Gentner (1996) Commonalities and differences in similarity comparisons
finding: Experiment 1 with picture pairs: listed alignable differences rose with similarity; listed nonalignable ones did not. Of 72 consensus alignable differences (listed by 5 or more people), all were clearly produced by a correspondence between the pictures.
numbers: Alignable differences by similarity: high M=3.20, medium M=2.97, low M=1.91 (high and medium above low, Bonferroni p<.05). Commonalities rose with similarity, F(2,29)=51.02, p<.001. Commonalities vs alignable r(14)=.69 (set 1) and .58 (set 2), both p<.05; vs nonalignable r(14)=-.06 (set 1). Rated similarity vs nonalignable count r=-.07 and .12, ns.
limits: With pictures the overall nonalignable count (M about 2.79) roughly equalled the alignable count (M about 2.70), which does not fit the claim that alignable differences dominate. The authors explain this by pictures making nonalignable items easy to list.
agent_relevance: Rich scenes release many nonalignable differences. Free diffing of complex outputs yields both kinds; code should tag which diffs sit inside the shared structure.

source: Markman & Gentner (1996) Commonalities and differences in similarity comparisons
finding: Experiment 2 gives the direct test: alignable differences lower rated similarity more than nonalignable differences. Similar vs dissimilar object pairs mattered only when the difference was alignable.
numbers: N=24 Columbia participants, within subjects, 8 stimulus sets. Nonalignable-difference pairs M=6.64 vs alignable M=5.61, F(1,7)=10.63, p<.05. Interaction F(1,7)=8.19, p<.05. Similar vs dissimilar nonalignable: 6.82 vs 6.46, t(7)=1.61, ns. Pilot forced choice: nonalignable option chosen on 88% of trials.
limits: Item analysis rests on only 8 sets (df=7). Pictures, college students. The pilot choice had a location confound.
agent_relevance: The effect depends on how unlike the matched objects are. A differing role-filler of a very different kind is a stronger signal.

source: Markman & Gentner (1996) Commonalities and differences in similarity comparisons
finding: Record of a failure in the program: in earlier word-pair studies the fourth prediction (alignable differences count more against similarity) was not supported. Regressions gave nonalignable differences equal or larger coefficients. The authors blame the regression method, which cannot separate commonalities from alignable differences.
numbers: Earlier word-pair regressions: rated similarity rose with commonalities and fell with differences, and the nonalignable coefficient was larger than the alignable one.
quote: However, the fourth prediction ... remains unsupported.
limits: This is the authors' own report of the earlier failure; resolved only by the later controlled design with a small item set.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'alignable differences matter most for similarity' as strongly replicated.

source: Kurtz & Gentner (2013) Detecting anomalous features in complex stimuli: the role of structured comparison
finding: Applied test with vertebrate skeleton drawings holding one wrong bone. A correct standard beside the target helps. A high-alignable standard (same orientation) beats a low-alignable one (mirror image) although both carry the same information.
numbers: Exp 1: N=75 (68 analysed), 27 triplets, within subjects. Accuracy: single M=0.61, low-alignable M=0.81, high-alignable M=0.87; F(2,134)=61.20, p<.001. High vs single d=1.86; low vs single d=1.43; high vs low t(67)=2.85, p<.01, d=0.43. RT on correct: single 6.76 s, low 10.65 s, high 9.96 s (high vs low ns).
limits: Told that exactly one bone was wrong. Mirror reversal also changes physical distance; a check found this did not explain the effect. Item differences were unexplained.
agent_relevance: Direct support for putting the right standard beside the target so the odd part stands out. Alignment quality matters, not only having a second example.

source: Kurtz & Gentner (2013) Detecting anomalous features in complex stimuli: the role of structured comparison
finding: Under a 13 s deadline the alignable-standard advantage is clearer; the low-alignable standard gives no reliable gain over the target alone.
numbers: Exp 2: N=58 (48 after exclusions). Accuracy single M=0.52, low M=0.57, high M=0.66; F(2,94)=7.42, p<.001. High vs single t(47)=3.89, d=0.82; high vs low t(47)=2.64, p<.01, d=0.53; single vs low p=.26, ns.
limits: Ten participants excluded for under 11 of 27 correct; the deadline made the task very hard.
agent_relevance: Under time or token pressure, only a well-aligned comparison pays off. Poorly aligned side-by-side examples can be wasted.

source: Kurtz & Gentner (2013) Detecting anomalous features in complex stimuli: the role of structured comparison
finding: Learning transfer: comparing anomalous targets with correct standards at study led to better detection on new single items than seeing the correct standards twice as often.
numbers: Exp 3: N=84, random assignment. Transfer test (10 novel items, 10 s deadline): comparison M=0.27 vs single M=0.14, t(82)=3.75, p<.001, d=0.86. Retest transfer: 0.36 vs 0.25, t(82)=2.76, p=.007, d=0.61. Old items: 0.52 vs 0.37, t(82)=3.23, p=.002, d=0.71.
limits: Absolute accuracy stays low (0.27 and 0.36). The authors cannot say whether learners acquired a skeletal schema, a list of likely errors, or an attention habit.
agent_relevance: Comparison leaves a reusable trace beyond the examples. Supports keeping aligned contrast pairs, not a pile of single good examples.

source: Kurtz & Gentner (2013) Detecting anomalous features in complex stimuli: the role of structured comparison
finding: Cites Kok et al. (2013): medical students studied chest radiographs; pathology/normal pairs beat pathology/pathology pairs on focal diseases. Also gives the speeded difference result as 'participants listed 3 times as many differences for high-similarity pairs'.
numbers: Kok et al.: pathology/normal M=0.63 vs pathology/pathology M=0.54 on focal diseases such as lung tumour; no effect on diffuse diseases (both groups did well).
limits: Second-hand for Kok et al. The '3 times' wording is looser than the 1994 raw means (about 2x).
agent_relevance: Contrast with a known-good case when the fault is local; other contrasts are needed when the fault is diffuse.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat undergraduates on most analogy sets: digit matrices, letter strings, four-term verbal analogies (UCLA VAT, Sternberg-Nigro, SAT, Jones). On story analogies (Gentner et al. materials) humans were clearly better; GPT-4 improved.
numbers: Letter-string humans N=57 UCLA. Story analogy humans N=54: GPT-3 chose the causal-structure target above chance in the near condition (binomial p=0.0039) but not the far condition (p=0.065); humans in far condition t(53)=16.7. Human vs GPT-3 OR=0.37, p=0.0003. 15 of 54 humans picked the analogous story on every trial. GPT-4 near-perfect in a first check.
limits: GPT-4 tested through a chat interface on 72 problems. GPT-3 may have seen letter-string tasks. Counterfactual tests (next line) weaken the generality claim.
agent_relevance: Models can find a relation shared across texts with different surface entities when asked, but are weaker in far (different domain) cases. Ask for the relation explicitly.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counterfactual letter-string analogies (permuted alphabets, symbol alphabets) break LLM performance but not human performance. A partial failure to extend Webb et al.
numbers: Humans N=134 (Prolific; 1,876 samples): accuracy 0.753 [0.734, 0.773]. GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Human accuracy stays flat across 0 to 20 permuted letters; GPT accuracy drops. Error types: GPT-3 'incorrect rule' 31% vs humans 15%; humans 'alternate rule' 39% vs GPT-3 6%.
limits: Zero-generalisation problems only. 2023-era GPT models; later reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Do not trust apparent relational reasoning on familiar forms. Test the comparison step on unfamiliar surface forms (mutated inputs, G3).

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Novel tasks where semantic concepts must be re-represented to map onto symbol patterns. The strongest post-trained models reach human level in the main conditions but differ from humans on controls and stress tests (misleading semantics, dual-attribute rules).
numbers: Human accuracy fell from about 0.7 (Categorial) to about 0.4 (Dual-attribute), coef=-1.23, z=-3.09, p=0.002; Numeric to compositional about 0.6 to 0.5, ns. Models did not show the same drop.
limits: Arbitrary novel tasks; small human samples (university recruits, $10). Authors call it a how-possibly model, not how-actually. Some conditions swung from near 0 to about 100% with small prompt changes.
agent_relevance: Structure mapping does not say how features are chosen; models can re-represent concepts yet behave unlike humans under distraction. Use code-checked held-out examples.

source: Stevenson & Pafford (2024) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near) and symbol (far) alphabets. Children and adults held performance across alphabets; each LLM dropped significantly from Latin to Greek and again to Symbol.
numbers: Adults N=68, children N=44 (age 7 to 9). Latin-to-Greek drop significant for every model (Bonferroni p<.001, except Llama-3.1 405B p=0.012). GPT-4o similar to adults on Latin; Claude 3.5 and Gemma-2 27B below children on Latin.
limits: Letter strings only; non-reasoning chat models; message-history setting changed results for some models.
agent_relevance: Transfer of relations to unfamiliar symbol sets is the weak point. Present contrast pairs in the task's own surface form.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Narrative benchmark separating surface mapping from system (relational) mapping. LLMs detect near analogies reasonably but fail on far analogies and are lured by surface-similar distractors.
numbers: Humans: near analogies 97.9%, far 94.1% (overall 96%). Models: near 75.0%, far 39.6% (below 50% chance). GPT-4 average 68.1%; SBERT average 42.3% and 1% when far analogies must beat near distractors.
limits: Zero-shot and few-shot; GPT-4 era; distractors built with an LLM plus human check. Explicit instructions to attend to system mappings helped somewhat.
agent_relevance: The alignable-versus-surface split in practice: LLMs weight surface overlap. A comparison step that names the shared relation first, then checks it in code, is safer than a bare similarity judgement.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: Deriving story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: 24K story pairs annotated for entity similarity and relation similarity (extended structure mapping). Analogy identification is very hard for LLMs; they prefer hard negatives with similar entities.
numbers: ChatGPT about 30% on 4-way multiple choice (random 25%, humans 85.7%). Models pick the analogous target in under 20% of cases against hard negatives where chance is 50%. Annotator agreement Fleiss kappa 47% (entity) and 42% (relation). Fine-tuning data raised LLaMa generation quality by +28.4% and +27.5%.
limits: Stories partly LLM-generated; kappa only moderate; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Another sign that surface similarity dominates model comparison. State the relation explicitly.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own related problems and solutions, then solves the target. It matches or beats few-shot chain of thought with no labelled exemplars.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0, 33.9, 34.9, 37.3. PaLM2 GSM8K: 60.8, 78.2, 80.7, 81.7. text-davinci-003 GSM8K: 14.8, 50.3, 54.0, 61.0. Gains also on Codeforces and BIG-Bench.
limits: GPT-3.5 GSM8K gain over few-shot CoT is only +1.1. Works with larger models; with smaller models retrieved exemplars did better. More output tokens. This tests retrieval of analogues, not comparison of two items.
agent_relevance: Self-generated analogues can replace hand-made exemplars for strong models only. Does not test comparison.

source: Chia et al. (2023) Contrastive chain-of-thought prompting
finding: Showing both a valid and an automatically made invalid reasoning chain for the same question improves chain of thought. Closest LLM analogue to comparing a correct and an incorrect case.
numbers: Table 2 (GPT-3.5): GSM8K CoT 69.2 to contrastive 79.0 (+9.8); GSM-Hard 33.8 to 44.2 (+10.4); SVAMP 67.2 to 81.6 (+14.4); ASDIV 70.8 to 84.4 (+13.6); Bamboogle 40.8 to 56.8 (+16.0); StrategyQA 55.8 to 66.2 (+10.4); AQuA 53.5 to 57.5. With self-consistency gains of +12.6 to +17.6.
limits: Invalid chains are made by editing valid ones (e.g. incoherent objects), so the pair is nearly minimal. Not compared against token-matched baselines. One model family.
agent_relevance: A valid chain beside a broken one is an aligned contrast. Supports S2 contrast steps with small local differences.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL: a benchmark for long text analogy evaluation
finding: Six-level analogy taxonomy (word, word vs sentence, syntactic, negation, entailment, metaphor), thirteen datasets, eight LLMs. Identifying analogies gets harder up the taxonomy.
numbers: Eight LLMs, three distance measures, thirteen datasets; exact scores not extracted.
limits: Only abstract and taxonomy read; embedding-distance based; weak link to alignable differences.
agent_relevance: Weak link only: relational similarity detection degrades with abstraction.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus & Gentner (1989) The structure-mapping engine (described in Gentner & Markman 1997)
finding: Original SME paper; cited by all the papers above for the local-to-global algorithm. Not opened; described via Gentner & Markman 1997.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: See the SME line above.

source: Kok et al. (2013) radiograph comparison study (cited by Kurtz & Gentner 2013)
finding: Cited second-hand: chest radiograph pairs with a normal image helped for focal diseases.
numbers: pathology/normal 0.63 vs pathology/pathology 0.54 on focal diseases (as reported by Kurtz & Gentner).
limits: Not opened; exact title and design not checked.
agent_relevance: Same as above.
